findings.description: The EC2 instance's user_data embeds a literal AWS access key ID and secret access key (AKIAIOSFODNN7EXAMAAA / wJalrXUtnFEMI/K7MDENG/bPxRfiCYEXAMAAAKEY) in cleartext. user_data is readable via the instance metadata service, the console, and the API, so these credentials are exposed to anyone with instance or metadata access.
The security group allows SSH (port 22) from 0.0.0.0/0, exposing the administrative interface to the entire internet and enabling brute-force or credential-based compromise.

The security group also permits HTTP (port 80) from 0.0.0.0/0. Given the instance is intentionally a public web host this is expected exposure, but the lack of any source restriction should be an explicit, deliberate decision. Reported as low.
The EBS volume attached to the portal server sets no encrypted attribute, so all data written to it is stored unencrypted at rest and snapshots taken from it inherit the unencrypted state.
The S3 bucket receiving VPC flow logs has no aws_s3_bucket_server_side_encryption_configuration, so flow log records are stored unencrypted at rest.

The bucket has no aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block and relies on legacy defaults. Because Terraform's aws_s3_bucket resource does not itself enable all four block-public-access settings and no ACL/policy hardening is present, a later ACL or policy change could render the flow-log archive publicly readable.

The instance serves the portal over Apache with only port 80 (HTTP) permitted by its security group; no TLS listener or certificate is configured, so web traffic to the portal is transmitted in cleartext.
